question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: The 'This computer' section. Exact tool versions, browser flags and stand-ins for the controller, touch device, listener and second player meant I could test the riskiest parts of the plan here instead of guessing. I also liked the split between firm requirements (dev mode, attract, 10-foot UI, the hub) and open choices (genre, perspective, effort): as director I knew what I could decide and what I could not.

question: What was confusing?
answer: Three things. (1) 'Follow [the hub] for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own' can mean the game must simply still run outside a session, or that it must also have multiplayer outside the hub. The protocol offers no transport outside a session, so I planned local same-screen co-op to cover both readings, but that was a guess. (2) The title riff and the file names are in TASK.md, while STAGE.md says to leave them out. That was clear enough once read together, but I had to decide whether the exit-interview file counts as one of the file names to leave out (I treated it as one). (3) TASK.md says python3 -m http.server prints the port, but when its output is piped it is block-buffered and prints nothing, so a script reading the port hangs until -u is added. Similarly, python3 -I hides the system Playwright, while the environment notes suggest -I for reading downloads. Both cost me a run. The listed Chromium flags also leave out --use-vulkan=swiftshader and --use-angle=swiftshader, which the engine's own docs recommend and which I used.

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Making a pointer-precision surgery game fit two things that pull against it: a controller at 10 feet, and an engine whose game hook assumes a walking player, a follow camera and a text-only HUD. Finding out what the plan had to demand meant reading the app, view and input code and then proving the approach with spikes. The hardest art call was the story characters: my first idea, SDF busts, looked like dolls, and I only found the paper-card approach by testing and rejecting it. Then came deciding how much of that to write down, so a builder who has never seen my spikes can succeed without being buried.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: State plainly whether multiplayer is required outside AI Hub, and if so what kind (local, or online through something other than the hub). Say how large the demo should be, even as a rough range of minutes or levels, because 'long enough to show ALL features' leaves a lot of scope to guess at and that scope drives the whole plan. Say whether the builder receives only the plan or also anything else the planner made, so the planner knows whether tested code must be pasted into the plan. Correct the http.server note (use python3 -u, read the first line) and list the full Chromium flag set that gives real pixels from a WebGPU canvas. Lastly, say whether planners may build and run the engine, since a few minutes of spikes changed several decisions in this plan.
